4.1. More powerful Natural Numbers🔗

Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00)

Is Basics needed explicitly? And why are these here instead of at the top of the file?

import LF.Basics
import LF.Induction

Until now, we have been working with our own custom natural numbers, using the Nat type that we defined in Basics.lean.

However, Lean has a built-in type of natural numbers, which is more powerful and comes with many useful features. They are very slightly different from our custom Nat, but these differences are mostly superficial. The built-in natural numbers are defined in the Init module, which is automatically imported by Lean. We will refer to them as Nat as well, but they are not the same as the Nat we defined in Basics.lean.

In Lean, programmers and mathematicians don't re-prove the basic properties of natural numbers from scratch, nor do they tend to write out rewrite steps for basic properties of natural numbers by hand.

Previously, we did computation like this...

theorem test_mult1' : (two * two : NatPlayground.Nat) = four := ⊢ two * two = four ⊢ zero.succ.succ * zero.succ.succ = four ⊢ zero + zero.succ.succ + zero.succ.succ = four ⊢ (zero + zero.succ.succ).succ.succ = four ⊢ zero.succ.succ.succ.succ = four All goals completed! 🐙 end long_example theorem test_mult1' : (two * two : NatPlayground.Nat) = four := ⊢ two * two = four ⊢ zero.succ.succ * zero.succ.succ = four ⊢ zero + zero.succ.succ + zero.succ.succ = four ⊢ (zero + zero.succ.succ).succ.succ = four ⊢ zero.succ.succ.succ.succ = four All goals completed! 🐙 end long_example theorem test_mult1' : (two * two : NatPlayground.Nat) = four := ⊢ two * two = four ⊢ zero.succ.succ * zero.succ.succ = four ⊢ zero + zero.succ.succ + zero.succ.succ = four ⊢ (zero + zero.succ.succ).succ.succ = four ⊢ zero.succ.succ.succ.succ = four All goals completed! 🐙 end long_example
Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, NOW)

The info viewed in the InfoView during this proof is kind of mysterious (to me) here. Have we already given people enough help to understand it here?

This approach is useful in a textbook for understanding the structure of natural numbers and for providing early practice with writing proofs. But it is also tedious in the long term.

Instead of doing this, programmers and mathematicians use the built-in Nat and the powerful features of Lean to automatically prove properties about natural numbers and to compute with them.

theorem test_mult1_nat : (3 * 3 : Nat) = 9 := ⊢ 3 * 3 = 9 All goals completed! 🐙 theorem test_mult1_nat : (3 * 3 : Nat) = 9 := ⊢ 3 * 3 = 9 All goals completed! 🐙 theorem test_mult1_nat : (3 * 3 : Nat) = 9 := ⊢ 3 * 3 = 9 All goals completed! 🐙

The annotation : Nat tells Lean that we are using its built-in Nat type.

In this chapter we will learn how to use the built-in Nat and some powerful features for computing with and proving properties about natural numbers. Specifically, we will learn about dsimp, calc, and simp annotations, which enable more powerful and concise proofs.

In fact, from now on, we will use the built-in Nat type and its powerful features, writing Nat.<theorem> to reference Lean's version of <theorem>.

4.1.1. rfl and computation with Nat🔗

With Lean's Nat, much of the computation happens automatically, and rfl suffices to close any equality of computation on literals.

theorem complicated_computation : (2 * 3 + 4 * 5 : Nat) * 6 = 156 := ⊢ (2 * 3 + 4 * 5) * 6 = 156 All goals completed! 🐙 theorem complicated_computation : (2 * 3 + 4 * 5 : Nat) * 6 = 156 := ⊢ (2 * 3 + 4 * 5) * 6 = 156 All goals completed! 🐙 theorem complicated_computation : (2 * 3 + 4 * 5 : Nat) * 6 = 156 := ⊢ (2 * 3 + 4 * 5) * 6 = 156 All goals completed! 🐙

This quickly becomes necessary, as natural numbers quickly get large!

Of course, rfl can't close more complicated goals where the values of the terms are unknown.

theorem rfl_not_enough (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ n = m -- rfl will not work here! /- First rewrite the goal with `h`; then the two sides are identical. -/ n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ m = m All goals completed! 🐙 theorem rfl_not_enough (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ n = m -- rfl will not work here! /- First rewrite the goal with `h`; then the two sides are identical. -/ n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ m = m All goals completed! 🐙 theorem rfl_not_enough (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ n = m -- rfl will not work here! /- First rewrite the goal with `h`; then the two sides are identical. -/ n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ m = m All goals completed! 🐙

The same proof can be written more compactly with rw. In this example, rw [h] rewrites with h and then closes the resulting reflexive goal.

theorem rfl_not_enough' (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ n = m All goals completed! 🐙 theorem rfl_not_enough' (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ n = m All goals completed! 🐙 theorem rfl_not_enough' (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := n:Natm:Nath:n = m⊢ n = m All goals completed! 🐙

We will continue to show more powerful tools for manipulating the context and goal of a proof to bring them closer to what can be solved with rfl.

4.2. Using the Standard Library🔗

Use the exact? tactic to search for relevant theorems in the standard library.

example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := a:Natb:Nat⊢ a + b = b + a /- this will suggest that we use `exact Nat.add_comm a b` to close this goal -/ All goals completed! 🐙 example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := a:Natb:Nat⊢ a + b = b + a /- this will suggest that we use `exact Nat.add_comm a b` to close this goal -/ Try this: [apply] exact Nat.add_comm a bAll goals completed! 🐙 example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := a:Natb:Nat⊢ a + b = b + a /- this will suggest that we use `exact Nat.add_comm a b` to close this goal -/ Try this: [apply] exact Nat.add_comm a bAll goals completed! 🐙

You can also use rw? to look for theorems to rewrite by

example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := a:Natb:Nat⊢ a + b = b + a /- this will suggest that we use `rw [Nat.add_comm]` to close this goal -/ All goals completed! 🐙 example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := a:Natb:Nat⊢ a + b = b + a /- this will suggest that we use `rw [Nat.add_comm]` to close this goal -/ Try this: [apply] rw [Nat.add_comm] -- no goalsAll goals completed! 🐙 example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := a:Natb:Nat⊢ a + b = b + a /- this will suggest that we use `rw [Nat.add_comm]` to close this goal -/ Try this: [apply] rw [Nat.add_comm] -- no goalsAll goals completed! 🐙 example (n m q : Nat) : (n + m) + q = m + (n + q) := n:Natm:Natq:Nat⊢ n + m + q = m + (n + q) -- lots of suggestions to look through here! n:Natm:Natq:Nat⊢ n + q + m = m + (n + q) All goals completed! 🐙 declaration uses `sorry`example (n m q : Nat) : (n + m) + q = m + (n + q) := n:Natm:Natq:Nat⊢ n + m + q = m + (n + q) -- lots of suggestions to look through here! 4.3. Structuring proofs with calc🔗

In Lean proofs, long rw chains are useful, but they are sometimes hard to read because the intermediate goals are invisible. Furthermore, sometimes we know exactly how we want to manipulate the terms of a proof, but don't want to have the tactics like add_comm and add_assoc "guess" which subterms to rewrite.

The calc tactic writes down the intermediate goals of a proof, and allows us to specify exactly which rewrite rules to apply at each step. It is a powerful tool for structuring proofs, and is often more readable than long rw chains.

calc is designed to mimic the style of proofs in mathematics textbooks, which will often look something like this:

a + (b + c)
= (a + b) + c        ...   [by associativity of addition]
= (b + a) + c        ...   [by commutativity of addition]
= b + (a + c)        ...   [by associativity of addition]

Note how we can see each intermediate step of this proof when we look at it this way. Let's look at how we might prove this theorem (i.e., that a + (b + c) = b + (a + c)) in Lean.

First, a proof in the style we already know.

theorem add_swap (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙 theorem add_swap (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙 theorem add_swap (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙

Here we present the same theorem, written with calc. Note how each intermediate goal is visible in the source.

theorem add_swap' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) calc a + (b + c) /- one side of the goal is the argument to `calc`... -/ /- ... and each subsequent line is a transformation, with a tactic. -/ a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = a + b + c All goals completed! 🐙 (a + b) + c = (b + a) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + b + c = b + a + c All goals completed! 🐙 /- once a line matches the other side of the equality in the main goal (in this case `(b + (a + c)`), the calc tactic succeeds. -/ (b + a) + c = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ b + a + c = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙 theorem add_swap' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) calc a + (b + c) /- one side of the goal is the argument to `calc`... -/ /- ... and each subsequent line is a transformation, with a tactic. -/ a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = a + b + c All goals completed! 🐙 (a + b) + c = (b + a) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + b + c = b + a + c All goals completed! 🐙 /- once a line matches the other side of the equality in the main goal (in this case `(b + (a + c)`), the calc tactic succeeds. -/ (b + a) + c = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ b + a + c = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙 theorem add_swap' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) calc a + (b + c) /- one side of the goal is the argument to `calc`... -/ /- ... and each subsequent line is a transformation, with a tactic. -/ a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = a + b + c All goals completed! 🐙 (a + b) + c = (b + a) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + b + c = b + a + c All goals completed! 🐙 /- once a line matches the other side of the equality in the main goal (in this case `(b + (a + c)`), the calc tactic succeeds. -/ (b + a) + c = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ b + a + c = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙

We can also write the proof like this to be a bit more concise:

theorem add_swap'' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) calc a + (b + c) _ = (a + b) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = a + b + c All goals completed! 🐙 _ = (b + a) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + b + c = b + a + c All goals completed! 🐙 _ = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ b + a + c = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙 theorem add_swap'' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) calc a + (b + c) _ = (a + b) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = a + b + c All goals completed! 🐙 _ = (b + a) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + b + c = b + a + c All goals completed! 🐙 _ = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ b + a + c = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙 theorem add_swap'' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) calc a + (b + c) _ = (a + b) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + (b + c) = a + b + c All goals completed! 🐙 _ = (b + a) + c := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ a + b + c = b + a + c All goals completed! 🐙 _ = b + (a + c) := a:Natb:Natc:Nat⊢ b + a + c = b + (a + c) All goals completed! 🐙

Whereas before, the left-hand side of each equality in the calc tactic was repeated from the right-hand side of the previous one, we can replace the left-hand side entirely with an _. Now our Lean proof looks quite a bit like the textbook one we saw earlier!

Exercise★(succ_mul_succ)
theorem succ_mul_succ (n m : Nat) : (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := n:Natm:Nat⊢ (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 All goals completed! 🐙 theorem succ_mul_succ (n m : Nat) : (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := n:Natm:Nat⊢ (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 All goals completed! 🐙 theorem succ_mul_succ (n m : Nat) : (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := n:Natm:Nat⊢ (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 All goals completed! 🐙

Given this proof with rw, rewrite it with calc. Reminder that you can use rw? to find appropriate rules to rewrite by.

theorem succ_mul_succ' (n m : Nat) : (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := n:Natm:Nat⊢ (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 solution! calc (n + 1) * (m + 1) _ = n * (m + 1) + 1 * (m + 1) := n:Natm:Nat⊢ (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * (m + 1) + 1 * (m + 1) All goals completed! 🐙 _ = n * (m + 1) + (m + 1) := n:Natm:Nat⊢ n * (m + 1) + 1 * (m + 1) = n * (m + 1) + (m + 1) All goals completed! 🐙 _ = (n * m + n * 1) + (m + 1) := n:Natm:Nat⊢ n * (m + 1) + (m + 1) = n * m + n * 1 + (m + 1) All goals completed! 🐙 _ = (n * m + n) + (m + 1) := n:Natm:Nat⊢ n * m + n * 1 + (m + 1) = n * m + n + (m + 1) All goals completed! 🐙 _ = n * m + n + m + 1 := n:Natm:Nat⊢ n * m + n + (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 All goals completed! 🐙 theorem declaration uses `sorry`succ_mul_succ' (n m : Nat) : (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := n:Natm:Nat⊢ (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 All goals completed! 🐙 theorem declaration uses `sorry`succ_mul_succ' (n m : Nat) : (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := n:Natm:Nat⊢ (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 All goals completed! 🐙

If you prefer rw to calc, that's fine! Each has particular uses, and both will be tools in your ever-growing toolbox of tactics.

4.4. Definitional simplification: dsimp🔗

Often, rather than rewriting by a known equation like

n + succ m = succ (n + m) using rw [add_succ],

we just want to simplify the function (here add) automatically when we can.

The dsimp tactic ("definitionally simplify") unfolds definitions and performs definitional simplifications. You can give it hints in square brackets: dsimp [f] tells it to unfold the definition of f. You can also simplify a hypothesis h in the context by writing dsimp [...] at h. dsimp will also close goals by rfl when possible.

def square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n def triple (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n + n def square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n def triple (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n + n def square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n def triple (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n + n

When the goal depends on a fact about an unknown value, rfl fails. Here, dsimp makes progress, exposing a goal the fact can close.

example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ triple n = m + n -- rfl will not work here! n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ n + n + n = m + n /- The goal can now be rewritten by `h`. -/ All goals completed! 🐙 example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ triple n = m + n -- rfl will not work here! n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ n + n + n = m + n /- The goal can now be rewritten by `h`. -/ All goals completed! 🐙 example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ triple n = m + n -- rfl will not work here! n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ n + n + n = m + n /- The goal can now be rewritten by `h`. -/ All goals completed! 🐙

As we have seen, rw can also unfold definitions. In this example, either style is fine: use dsimp [triple] when you want to emphasize definitional simplification, or rw [triple, h] when the proof is just a sequence of rewrites.

example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ triple n = m + n /- `rw [triple]` unfolds `triple n`. -/ All goals completed! 🐙 example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ triple n = m + n /- `rw [triple]` unfolds `triple n`. -/ All goals completed! 🐙 example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m⊢ triple n = m + n /- `rw [triple]` unfolds `triple n`. -/ All goals completed! 🐙
Exercise★★(dsimp1)

Complete this proof, using dsimp or rw as appropriate.

example (n m : Nat) (h : m = n) : triple m = n + (n + n) := n:Natm:Nath:m = n⊢ triple m = n + (n + n) solution! n:Natm:Nath:m = n⊢ triple n = n + (n + n) n:Natm:Nath:m = n⊢ n + n + n = n + (n + n) All goals completed! 🐙 declaration uses `sorry`example (n m : Nat) (h : m = n) : triple m = n + (n + n) := n:Natm:Nath:m = n⊢ triple m = n + (n + n) All goals completed! 🐙 declaration uses `sorry`example (n m : Nat) (h : m = n) : triple m = n + (n + n) := n:Natm:Nath:m = n⊢ triple m = n + (n + n) All goals completed! 🐙

dsimp at h also works on hypotheses, which rfl can't touch.

example (n : Nat) (h : square n = 16) : n * n = 16 := n:Nath:square n = 16⊢ n * n = 16 n:Nath:n * n = 16⊢ n * n = 16 All goals completed! 🐙 example (n : Nat) (h : square n = 16) : n * n = 16 := n:Nath:square n = 16⊢ n * n = 16 n:Nath:n * n = 16⊢ n * n = 16 All goals completed! 🐙 example (n : Nat) (h : square n = 16) : n * n = 16 := n:Nath:square n = 16⊢ n * n = 16 n:Nath:n * n = 16⊢ n * n = 16 All goals completed! 🐙

Aside: rw [...] at h also works on hypotheses too, as does rw? at h

example (n m : Nat) (h : 2 * n = m * 2) : n + n = m + m := n:Natm:Nath:2 * n = m * 2⊢ n + n = m + m n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m + m⊢ n + n = m + m All goals completed! 🐙 example (n m : Nat) (h : 2 * n = m * 2) : n + n = m + m := n:Natm:Nath:2 * n = m * 2⊢ n + n = m + m n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m + m⊢ n + n = m + m All goals completed! 🐙 example (n m : Nat) (h : 2 * n = m * 2) : n + n = m + m := n:Natm:Nath:2 * n = m * 2⊢ n + n = m + m n:Natm:Nath:n + n = m + m⊢ n + n = m + m All goals completed! 🐙

dsimp also takes definitional steps such as + 0, so it can finish goals that rfl would close.

example (n : Nat) : square n + 0 = n * n := n:Nat⊢ square n + 0 = n * n All goals completed! 🐙 example (n : Nat) : square n + 0 = n * n := n:Nat⊢ square n + 0 = n * n All goals completed! 🐙 example (n : Nat) : square n + 0 = n * n := n:Nat⊢ square n + 0 = n * n All goals completed! 🐙

Like rw and exact, dsimp also has a ? version that searches for functions to simplify by. Many Lean tactics have ? versions; try it out if you are unsure.

4.5. Redefining Functions and Lemmas over Nats🔗

Let's redefine some functions on Lean's Nats and prove some theorems about them.

def Nat.even (n : Nat) := match n with | 0 => true | 1 => false | n + 2 => even n def Nat.odd (n : Nat) := !(even n) theorem Nat.odd_def (n : Nat) : n.odd = !(n.even) := rfl def Nat.minustwo (n : Nat) : Nat := match n with | 0 => 0 | 1 => 0 | n' + 2 => n' def Nat.double (n : Nat) : Nat := match n with | 0 => 0 | n' + 1 => double n' + 2 def Nat.even (n : Nat) := match n with | 0 => true | 1 => false | n + 2 => even n def Nat.odd (n : Nat) := !(even n) theorem Nat.odd_def (n : Nat) : n.odd = !(n.even) := rfl def Nat.minustwo (n : Nat) : Nat := match n with | 0 => 0 | 1 => 0 | n' + 2 => n' def Nat.double (n : Nat) : Nat := match n with | 0 => 0 | n' + 1 => double n' + 2 def Nat.even (n : Nat) := match n with | 0 => true | 1 => false | n + 2 => even n def Nat.odd (n : Nat) := !(even n) theorem Nat.odd_def (n : Nat) : n.odd = !(n.even) := rfl def Nat.minustwo (n : Nat) : Nat := match n with | 0 => 0 | 1 => 0 | n' + 2 => n' def Nat.double (n : Nat) : Nat := match n with | 0 => 0 | n' + 1 => double n' + 2

Defining functions in the Nat namespace changes how they print:

theorem even_add_three (n : Nat) : Nat.even (n + 3) = Nat.even (n + 1) := n:Nat⊢ (n + 3).even = (n + 1).even All goals completed! 🐙 theorem even_add_three (n : Nat) : Nat.even (n + 3) = Nat.even (n + 1) := n:Nat⊢ (n + 3).even = (n + 1).even All goals completed! 🐙 theorem even_add_three (n : Nat) : Nat.even (n + 3) = Nat.even (n + 1) := n:Nat⊢ (n + 3).even = (n + 1).even All goals completed! 🐙

This printing style is called field notation and can be disabled with the pp_nodot attribute.

example (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := n:Nat⊢ (n + 0).double = n.double All goals completed! 🐙 attribute [pp_nodot] Nat.double example (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := n:Nat⊢ Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n All goals completed! 🐙 example (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := n:Nat⊢ (n + 0).double = n.double All goals completed! 🐙 attribute [pp_nodot] Nat.double example (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := n:Nat⊢ Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n All goals completed! 🐙 example (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := n:Nat⊢ (n + 0).double = n.double All goals completed! 🐙 attribute [pp_nodot] Nat.double example (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := n:Nat⊢ Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n All goals completed! 🐙

4.6. Using Code Actions to Generate Match Skeletons🔗

Lean's language server can suggest code actions, which are small editor commands that modify the source code. In VSCode, a light-bulb icon appears on the left when a code action is available at your cursor. You can click the icon or open the code action menu with Ctrl + . on Windows/Linux or Command + . on macOS.

For more information, see [Lean 4 VS Code extension manual](https://github.com/leanprover/vscode-lean4/blob/master/vscode-lean4/manual/manual.md#code-actions).

Some code actions can generate the explicit branches needed for pattern matching. This is especially useful when working with match expressions, or with tactics such as cases and induction, which we saw in previous chapters.

Let's look at an example using induction.

←3. Induction: Proof by Induction5. Lists: Working with Structured Data→
